Unit 10 — Monochromatic Color and Value — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q3 · Unit 10 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work: Pablo Picasso, Mother and Child, 1902, Harvard Art Museums / Fogg Museum (IN COPYRIGHT — link-out only)

Studio project / ladder rung: Monochromatic Disco Ball — variation rung (study Picasso's one-color modeling, then apply tint-to-shade to a round object of the student's own)

REVISION NOTE (this pass)

This unit was revised from the 03_Development draft per the subject-matter reviewer's note and the shared revision brief. What changed and why:

  • Featured work swapped: the draft used Picasso's The Old Guitarist (Art Institute of Chicago). Per the brief, this unit now features Picasso's Mother and Child (1902, Harvard Art Museums / Fogg Museum) instead. Picasso painted several works titled Mother and Child across different periods; this one was chosen because it is a verified, real Blue Period work (confirmed via Harvard Art Museums' own collection record, object 299993) and keeps the unit's monochromatic-value pedagogy intact — it is painted almost entirely in blue, exactly like the work it replaces. All Look First / DAIJ / Quick Check-in / Part 2 example-caption text was rewritten to describe this painting instead of The Old Guitarist. Copyright tier (in-copyright, link-out only) is unchanged.
  • VR Session redesigned: replaced the "load a pre-made snapshot" pattern with a pick-your-own-work pattern. Students now choose from 2 real, verified, public-domain monochromatic works (or bring their own, teacher-approved), pull the chosen image into their own VR space, and run DAIJ on it themselves.
  • Part 2 imagery (value scale, tint/shade/tone cards, sphere-vs-flat-disc demo) is original HTML/CSS/SVG built with course design tokens; nothing photographic or AI-generated appears, so no change was needed there beyond the caption text touch-up noted above.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q3 set)

  • VA.912.C.1.4 — Apply art knowledge and contextual information to analyze how content and ideas are used in works of art (the monochromatic/Blue Period reading of Mother and Child; DAIJ).
  • VA.912.O.3.2 — Analyze the organizational principles and structural elements used to create unity, contrast, and a focal point in works of art (one hue for unity; value contrast to keep the work alive).

Other Q3 map standards are carried across Units 9, 11, 12, 13. See course-shared standards tracker.

Cycle: Q3 · Unit 12 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week
Featured work: Aaron Douglas, Aspects of Negro Life: From Slavery to Reconstruction, 1934, Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, The New York Public Library (in copyright — link-out only)
Studio project / ladder rung: Storytelling Silhouette Landscape — variation rung
Focus: silhouette, flat shape, positive/negative space, value gradation, emphasis (focal point), contrast; Harlem Renaissance context.

REVISION NOTE (this pass)

This unit was revised from the 03_Development draft per the shared revision brief. What changed and why:

  • Featured work confirmed, title corrected. The brief asked us to verify Douglas is a real, museum-held, in-copyright work before keeping it. Re-verified directly against the NYPL Digital Collections page (digitalcollections.nypl.org/items/634ad849-7832-309e-e040-e00a180639bb): the work's exact title is "Aspects of Negro Life: From Slavery to Reconstruction" — the 03_Development draft had it as "...From Slavery Through Reconstruction," a small wording error. Corrected throughout lesson.html (mural title line and figcaption) and here. Everything else about the citation (artist, date, medium, holding institution, in-copyright status, NYPL link) was already accurate and has been kept as-is.
    • Note for the record: NYPL's own rights statement on this item currently reads "public domain under the laws of the United States" (citing the work's Public Works of Art Project origin), but per course policy (build-conventions.md's locked in-copyright list, which names Aaron Douglas explicitly) this unit continues to treat the work conservatively as in-copyright and link-out only, rather than embedding on the strength of one rights note. This matches the brief's explicit instruction to keep Douglas in-copyright/link-out.
  • VR Session redesigned: replaced the "load a pre-made snapshot" pattern with a pick-your-own-work pattern. Because the featured work is in copyright, the two VR example works given to students are both public domain and safe to pull directly into a VR space: an Attic black-figure amphora attributed to Exekias (Metropolitan Museum of Art, ca. 540 BCE — the historical origin of silhouette-as-technique), and Henri Rousseau's The Sleeping Gypsy (MoMA, 1897 — near-silhouette shapes and glowing value gradation). Students may also bring their own teacher-approved choice.

Unit 14: Chuck Close and the Grid Method: Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only: never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas
Cycle: Q4 · Unit 14 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week
Featured work: Chuck Close, Study for Self-Portrait, 1968, The Museum of Modern Art, New York (in copyright: link-out only). Companion reference: Big Self-Portrait, 1967 to 68, Walker Art Center, Minneapolis.
Studio project / ladder rung: Grid Enlargement Drawing: study/copy then variation rung

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q4 set)

  • VA.912.O.1.4: Apply the elements of art and principles of design to solve a specific visual art problem (proportion, scale, and unity, solved through the grid enlargement).
  • VA.912.S.3.3: Use materials, tools, and processes to develop skills/craftsmanship in a 2-D work (gridding, transfer, and value rendering by hand).
  • VA.912.C.2.4: Use accurate art vocabulary to evaluate a work in progress and revise it (consistent cell-to-cell value to achieve unity; DAIJ critique).

Other Q4 map standards are carried across the remaining Q4 units (15 and 16). See course-shared standards tracker.

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Learn & Look ≈ 250 min): lesson page reading + visuals (~55 min) · Sketch: Grid Copy Warm-Up (~40 min) · VR Photorealism and Grid Gallery Critique (~30 min) · Quiz + review (~20 min) · independent studio prep, choosing and gridding a reference, building the enlarged grid (~105 min).
Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Grid Enlargement Drawing studio work + artist statement (the graded assessment). Self-paced across the week. Cell-by-cell rendering is time-intensive; remind students to keep grid lines light and values consistent.

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Grid Enlargement Drawing + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Sketch, VR, and quiz are completion- or auto-scored.

Quiz answer key (Type A: Elements/Principles)

1-B · 2-C · 3-B · 4-C · 5-B · 6-True · 7 (Proportion→relative size of parts to one another and the whole; Grid method→copying square for square to stay accurate; Unity→all parts belong together as one; Scale→size compared to a standard such as the human body) · 8-B.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • Chuck Close (d. 2021) is IN COPYRIGHT. Do NOT embed any Close image anywhere in the lesson, Canvas items, or VR snapshot. Treat exactly like the Unit 6 Matisse pattern: link out only.
  • Verified 2026-07-15 via web search against MoMA's own collection listing: moma.org/collection/works/37904 is real and correctly attributed to Study for Self-Portrait (1968). MoMA's own description gives the medium as gelatin silver print, ink, pencil, and pressure-sensitive tape on board (a gift of Norman Dubrow). This is corrected from the prior draft, which did not list a medium.
  • Important factual correction made this pass: the prior draft's Part 1 description ("a huge black-and-white head... built up square by square") actually describes Big Self-Portrait (1967 to 68), the finished nine-by-seven-foot painting at the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, not the MoMA work this unit links to. Study for Self-Portrait is itself the small grid document, the actual photograph Close ruled a grid onto by hand as the working tool for enlarging the image onto that much larger canvas. The lesson now describes the linked MoMA work accurately (a gridded, marked-up photograph) and names Big Self-Portrait separately, in the figcaption and DAIJ, as the monumental painting it produced. This is a stronger teaching example than the original draft realized: it is literally the grid-method artifact, not just a finished result.
  • The lesson page presents Study for Self-Portrait by museum link to MoMA (moma.org/collection/works/37904) inside a link-card, with full citation (artist nationality + dates, title, date, medium, holding institution, rights status "© Chuck Close"). Big Self-Portrait (Walker Art Center) is named in the caption and DAIJ as the painting this study produced, not embedded.
  • DAIJ is conducted by verbal description of the actual linked work (a black-and-white photograph of Close's face with a hand-ruled ink grid, pencil notes, and tape), never by reproducing the image.
  • All inline visuals are original HTML/CSS/SVG built with the course design tokens (the gridded-image transfer demo and the single magnified cell), explicitly labeled "concept illustration, not Chuck Close's artwork." No third-party images, no AI-generated images.
  • VR gallery pool (redesigned this pass): students now choose and pull in their own image rather than loading a pre-made snapshot. Three verified, public-domain/cultural works are offered: an Ancient Egyptian wooden drawing board with a squared proportion grid (Dynasty 18, The British Museum, unknown artist), Albrecht Dürer's woodcut Draughtsman Drawing a Reclining Woman (1525, from his Painter's Manual), and William Michael Harnett's trompe l'oeil still life After the Hunt (1885, The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens). No Close image is loaded into VR; if a student proposes a different work, the teacher approves it before use.

Part 2 illustrative example: animal vs. human face (reviewer note)

  • Choice made: swapped, not added alongside. The prior draft's small-grid/large-grid transfer diagram used an ambiguous abstract oval with two dot "eyes," which read as a vague, slightly uncanny pseudo-face rather than a clean, purposeful illustration, exactly the "AI-feel" the course-wide image policy asks us to avoid in Part 2 concept art. It has been replaced with an original cat-face diagram (triangular ears, round eyes, a simple nose and mouth), built from the same clean geometric shapes as the rest of the course's original SVG diagrams.
  • Reasoning for a full swap rather than "both": the point of this particular diagram is just to make the grid-transfer concept instantly legible at a glance; a single clear illustrative subject does that better than a cluttered pair. Parity between animal and human subjects is preserved at the assignment level instead: the Studio Project materials line already explicitly offers "a printed photo of an animal or a face" as the reference image, so students choosing a human subject for their own graded artwork are still fully supported; the concept diagram simply demonstrates the mechanic with a subject that reads unambiguously in a small SVG.
  • The separate "one magnified cell" illustration was left as originally built (an abstract light/dark field with no recognizable feature), since it already deliberately avoids depicting any specific subject; its caption was updated only to note it has "no fur pattern" either, keeping it neutral to both animal and human readings.

Deployment notes

  • lesson.html → GitHub Pages, embed in Canvas via iframe (see canvas-interactive-widgets). Deploy-ready; no preview banner.
  • canvas-items.md → build each item Canvas-native (Quiz as a Canvas Quiz; Sketch/VR/Project as Canvas Assignments). Quiz Q8 image placeholder = an original small-grid / large-grid animal-face diagram (build-team asset, matching the lesson.html cat-face diagram), not a Close image.
  • Module intro/outro wrappers (Canvas-native quizzes) bracket the cycle per optima-canvas-assignments: built at module level, not in this unit folder.

Revision notes (this pass, 2026-07-15)

  • Re-verified the MoMA URL and corrected the medium and Part 1/DAIJ description to accurately match the actual linked work (Study for Self-Portrait, the grid maquette) rather than conflating it with Big Self-Portrait (the finished painting). See "Copyright check" above for detail.
  • Redesigned the VR Session to the course-wide student-chooses-and-loads-it-themselves pattern, replacing the old "load the Unit 14 gallery snapshot" instruction. Three real, verified, public-domain example works are offered (Egyptian grid board, Dürer woodcut, Harnett trompe l'oeil).
  • Swapped the Part 2 grid-transfer illustrative diagram from an ambiguous abstract human-face blob to a clear original cat-face diagram, per the reviewer's animal-subject note. Full reasoning above.
  • Studio Project, rubric, quiz, and sketch assignment content are unchanged in structure; the Studio Project's existing "animal or a face" reference-image option already gave students subject choice, so no change was needed there.

pages.html:
Unit 15 — Renaissance Perspective — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q4 · Unit 15 of 16 · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work: The Ideal City, anonymous painter, Central Italy, c. 1480 to 1490, Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, Urbino (public domain)

Focus: Space (linear perspective), with line and balance

Studio project / ladder rung: Two-Point Perspective Cityscape — study/copy (sketch) then variation (project)

REVISION NOTE (2026-07-15)

This unit was revised against the shared revision brief. Two changes from the 03_Development draft:

  1. Attribution language verified and tightened. Checked against Wikipedia's The Ideal City (painting) article, the painting's own holding museum (Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, gndm.it/en/opere/citta-ideale/), and the Wikimedia Commons file page. The museum's own catalog entry lists the artist as “Anonimo Artista dell'Italia Centrale” (anonymous Central Italian artist); the work was formerly attributed to Piero della Francesca, and the architect Luciano Laurana, Francesco di Giorgio Martini, and Melozzo da Forlì have all been separately proposed. Confirmed dimensions (67.7 x 239.4 cm), medium (oil on panel), and date range (1480 to 1490). The lesson and this plan now say “anonymous painter... formerly attributed to...” rather than naming Piero della Francesca as if settled. The embedded Wikimedia image itself was already correctly sourced and did not need to change.
  2. VR Session redesigned per the cross-cutting brief: instead of loading a pre-made Canvas snapshot, students now choose ONE of three real, verified Renaissance perspective works (Masaccio's Holy Trinity, Perugino's Delivery of the Keys, or Raphael's The School of Athens — all confirmed via web search as real, correctly dated, public-domain frescoes with well-documented one-point perspective), look it up, pull an image of it into their own VR space, and run the DAIJ critique on their own chosen piece. A teacher-approved own-choice option remains available. The VR Session's overall shape (Before You Enter / Look / Make / Submit / completion grading) is unchanged.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q4 set)

  • VA.912.O.3.3 — Analyze the organizational principles in works of art (here: space/perspective and balance) and their effect on the viewer.
  • VA.912.S.3.5 — Apply two-dimensional techniques and processes (linear perspective construction) to create works that communicate a sense of space.
  • VA.912.H.3.2 — Analyze how the creative and innovative ideas of a time and place (Renaissance Italy's reasoned, geometric approach to space) are reflected in artworks.

Confirm exact wording against the course-shared standards tracker; codes are placed per the Q4 distribution noted in the build brief.

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Learn & Look ≈ 250 min): lesson page reading + perspective diagrams (~55 min) · Sketch: Horizon, Two Points, and Boxes (~40 min) · VR Renaissance Perspective Gallery (choose-and-critique own work) + build (~35 min) · Quiz + review (~20 min) · independent perspective practice and cityscape planning/thumbnails (~100 min).

Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Two-Point Perspective Cityscape studio work + artist statement (the graded assessment). Self-paced across the week. Encourage students to lock the horizon line and both vanishing points before committing any building edges.

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Two-Point Perspective Cityscape + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Sketch, VR, and quiz are completion- or auto-scored.

Quiz answer key (Type B — Art History, blended with vocabulary)

1-B · 2-C · 3-B · 4-D · 5-A · 6-True · 7 (Horizon line→horizontal line at eye level; Vanishing point→where receding parallel lines appear to meet; Orthogonal lines→the slanting lines that run to a vanishing point; Two-point perspective→perspective using two vanishing points, for corner views) · 8-B.

Type rotation check: Unit 1 was Type A (Elements/Principles). Type B here satisfies the no-two-of-a-kind-back-to-back rule; confirm the adjacent Q4 unit is not also Type B.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • The Ideal City (Central Italian, c. 1480 to 1490, panel decades before any copyright cutoff) is public domain. The Wikimedia Commons file is a faithful photographic reproduction of a 2-D PD work. May be displayed in full with attribution + source link.
  • Attribution is honestly noted as debated, and verified against primary sources:
    • Wikipedia, The Ideal City (painting): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ideal_City_(painting) — notes the work was formerly attributed to Piero della Francesca, with Luciano Laurana, Francesco di Giorgio Martini, and Melozzo da Forlì all proposed by different scholars.
    • Official museum page, Galleria Nazionale delle Marche: https://gndm.it/en/opere/citta-ideale/ — the museum itself catalogs the work as by an anonymous Central Italian painter (“Anonimo Artista dell'Italia Centrale”), 1480 to 1490, oil on panel, 67.7 x 239.4 cm.
    • Wikimedia Commons file page confirms public-domain status and the file's title, which itself preserves the “formerly attributed to Piero della Francesca” language: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Formerly_Piero_della_Francesca_-_Ideal_City_-_WGA17633_-_Galleria_Nazionale_delle_Marche_Urbino.jpg
    • No invented sole author is asserted anywhere on the student page.
  • Embedded via Wikimedia Special:FilePath (license-checked against the file's Commons page before build). No in-copyright artists appear in this unit.
  • All inline visuals (the horizon/vanishing-point one-point diagram and the two-point box diagram) are original HTML/CSS/SVG built with design tokens — no third-party images, no AI-generated images.
  • VR Session example artworks (Masaccio Holy Trinity, c. 1427, Santa Maria Novella; Perugino Delivery of the Keys, 1481 to 1482, Sistine Chapel; Raphael The School of Athens, 1509 to 1511, Apostolic Palace) are all centuries-old frescoes by long-deceased artists — fully public domain — verified via web search against standard art-historical sources before being named to students.

Deployment notes

  • lesson.html → GitHub Pages, embed in Canvas via iframe (see canvas-interactive-widgets). Deploy-ready; no preview banner. Head/style/script/header copied verbatim from Unit-01 for byte consistency.
  • canvas-items.md → build each item Canvas-native (Quiz as a Canvas Quiz; Sketch/VR/Project as Canvas Assignments).
  • Q8 image: drop in a clean export of the lesson's one-point perspective SVG diagram, or rebuild a simple equivalent in the quiz tool.
  • VR Session: no pre-made Canvas snapshot file needs to be prepared or maintained anymore; students source their own reference image per the three named options (or a teacher-approved substitute).

Unit 16 — Mixed Media and Blackout Poetry — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q4 · Unit 16 of 16 (final unit) · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work: William Blake, The Tyger, plate from Songs of Experience, Copy A, hand-colored relief etching, designed and first printed 1794, British Museum, London (PUBLIC DOMAIN — embedded)

Studio project / ladder rung: Illustrated Blackout Poetry — variation toward invention

REVISION NOTE (2026-07-15) — what changed and why

The reviewer flagged a standalone copyright concern on this unit ("I think we need new imagery because of copyright"), with no specific replacement named. On inspection, the 03_Development draft's featured/anchor work was Tom Phillips's A Humument (begun 1966; Phillips, British, 1937 to 2022) — a still-very-much-in-copyright artist whose work was already handled as a link-out-only card (no embedded image), which is the correct treatment for an in-copyright work, but evidently still read to the reviewer as too much exposure for the course's one truly "final, anchor" unit-defining artwork, and it left the unit without any real embedded image at all (Part 1's whole point, "Look First," could not actually happen on this page).

Fix: Replaced Tom Phillips/A Humument as the featured/anchor work with William Blake's The Tyger (plate from Songs of Experience, designed and first printed 1794; Blake died 1827, fully public domain by any measure). This is a real, verified, embeddable image (Wikimedia Commons, sourced from the British Museum's own Copy A) that still serves the same Elements/Principles focus (line, shape, value, contrast, unity) and the same "text and image can become one unified page" idea at the heart of this unit. It has the added benefit of letting Part 1 "Look First" and Part 3 "Watch It Work / DAIJ" run directly on a visible image for the first time in this unit, instead of the workaround of describing an artwork only in words because it could not be shown.

Tom Phillips and A Humument are now mentioned by name and date only, in one sentence of body text, purely as the historical origin of the term "blackout poetry" (the term the studio project itself is built around). No image of the work appears anywhere on the page, and no dedicated link-out card, museum citation block, or .art-fig figure is built around it; this is a plain factual mention, which carries no image-rights exposure at all, and is a lighter touch than the 03_Development draft's link-out card.

Sources checked before building (WebSearch):

  • William Blake's Songs of Innocence and of Experience confirmed public domain worldwide, first published 1789 to 1794, illuminated books engraved/printed/hand-colored by Blake himself.
  • Wikimedia Commons file confirmed to exist: File:The_Tyger_BM_a_1794.jpg — William Blake, The Tyger, Copy A, British Museum, London, tagged public domain (life + 100 years or fewer). Direct file: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Tyger_BM_a_1794.jpg
  • "The Lamb" (Metropolitan Museum of Art / British Museum / Library of Congress / Fitzwilliam / Houghton copies), "The Blossom" (Google Art Project scan on Commons), and "The Little Black Boy" (Google Art Project scan on Commons) were each confirmed as real, existing Blake plates before being offered as VR-Session choices.

VR Session also redesigned per the cross-cutting brief and the unit-specific note that its example artworks must be copyright-safe: instead of loading a pre-made Canvas snapshot, students now choose ONE of four verified public-domain Blake plates (The Tyger, The Lamb, The Blossom, The Little Black Boy), look it up, pull an image into their own VR space, and run DAIJ on it. A teacher-approved own-choice option remains, restricted to public-domain work. The VR Session's Part 2 "Make" step (blacking out words in the air) and Part 3 "Respond" step are unchanged, since they practice the studio project's own skill regardless of which anchor artwork is used.

No other content in this unit (Sketch, Quiz, Studio Project, rubric) required a copyright fix; those were already correctly scoped to public-domain or student-owned text.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (from course map, Q4 set)

  • VA.912.C.3.3 — Examine relationships among social, historical, literary, and other references to explain how they support a creative interpretation of an artwork (word-and-image relationships in Blake's illuminated printing and in blackout poetry; using found/literary text as source).
  • VA.912.F.2.2 — Examine the effects that the visual arts have on culture and the world of work (artists who fuse text and image, from Blake's era to contemporary mixed-media practice).
  • VA.912.S.3.3 — Use materials, tools, and techniques in a safe and responsible manner during the creative process (mixed-media handling; lawful use of source text — public-domain or own only).

This is the final unit; it intentionally re-integrates line, shape, value, contrast, and unity from across the year rather than introducing a new isolated element.

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Learn & Look ≈ 250 min): lesson page reading + visuals (~55 min) · Sketch: Find the Poem, including choosing a public-domain or self-written page (~40 min) · VR Text-Art Gallery Critique, choosing and sourcing a Blake plate (~30 min) · Quiz + review (~20 min) · independent studio planning, sourcing a public-domain page, drafting word-paths (~105 min).

Week 2 (Make & Reflect ≈ 250 min): Illustrated Blackout Poetry studio work + artist statement (the graded assessment). Self-paced across the week. Remind students that sourcing the page legally is part of the timeline; they should have it chosen by end of Week 1.

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Illustrated Blackout Poetry page + artist statement on the 5-row rubric (~5 min/student). Sketch, VR, and quiz are completion- or auto-scored.

Quiz answer key

1-B · 2-C · 3-B · 4-A · 5-B · 6-True · 7 (Mixed media→combining more than one material on a single surface; Contrast→a strong difference between two things placed near each other; Unity→the sense that all parts belong together as one whole; Blackout poetry→keeping a few words on an existing page and covering the rest) · 8-B.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026) — TWO points, both critical

  1. William Blake (English, 1757 to 1827) is fully PUBLIC DOMAIN. The Tyger (Copy A, British Museum) is embedded directly via Wikimedia Commons Special:FilePath, license-checked against the file's Commons page (public domain, life + 100 years or fewer) before build. Full .art-fig figure/figcaption citation given: artist, nationality/dates, title, plate/copy, medium, date, holding institution, rights status, source link — matching the Unit-01/Unit-15 pattern. DAIJ is run directly on the visible image.

    • No image of Tom Phillips's A Humument appears anywhere on the page. Phillips (British, 1937 to 2022) and the 1966-begun A Humument project are mentioned once, by name and date only, as historical context for the term "blackout poetry." This is a factual citation, not a reproduction, and carries no rights exposure. Confirm during deploy that no Phillips image is ever substituted in.
    • VR Session example artworks (The Tyger, The Lamb, The Blossom, The Little Black Boy) are all verified public-domain Blake plates, held across the British Museum, Metropolitan Museum of Art, Library of Congress, Fitzwilliam Museum, and Houghton Library.

  2. Student source text must be PUBLIC-DOMAIN or the student's OWN writing, never a copyrighted page. This is stated in both the Sketch and the Studio Project student text, and is graded in the rubric's Artist Statement and Completion rows. Blacking out a copyrighted page produces a derivative work the student is not free to create or share. Suggested sources named for students: Project Gutenberg, public-domain newspaper archives (e.g., Library of Congress Chronicling America), or the student's own writing. Pre-1928 = safe public-domain cutoff used in student text.

  3. All non-photographic inline visuals are original HTML/CSS/SVG. The blackout mockup uses ORIGINAL placeholder text written for this lesson (kept words: river / light / stayed / turn / tide) and is clearly labeled a concept illustration. The weak-vs-strong unity demo uses original abstract shapes. The el-grid Line/Shape/Value/Contrast cards use original SVG. No AI-generated images anywhere in the unit.

AI-awareness note

The lesson's AI callout is factual only (AI can generate a poem or erase text in an image, but cannot make the choices about which found words and which marks carry meaning). No persuasive closer. Consistent with awareness-not-requirement policy.

Deployment notes

  • lesson.html → GitHub Pages, embed in Canvas via iframe (see canvas-interactive-widgets). Deploy-ready; no preview banner. Head/style/script/header copied verbatim from Unit-01 for byte-consistency.
  • canvas-items.md → build each item Canvas-native (Quiz as a Canvas Quiz; Sketch/VR/Project as Canvas Assignments).
  • Q8 image placeholder is flagged [IMAGE: ...]; build team supplies an original simple diagram (blacked-out page with five kept words joined by a line). Must be original art, not a reproduction of Blake's or Phillips's work.
  • VR Session: no pre-made Canvas snapshot file needs to be prepared or maintained anymore; students source their own reference image from the four named Blake plates (or a teacher-approved public-domain substitute).
  • As the final unit, the module outro wrapper should also close the year/course per optima-canvas-assignments — built at module level, not in this unit folder.

pages.html:
Unit 17 — Portfolio & Art Show — Teacher Cycle Plan

Teacher-facing. Benchmark codes and answer keys live here only — never on student pages.

Course: 2-D Studio Art · CPALMS 0101300 · Grades 9–12 · Full-year, async Canvas

Cycle: Q4 · Unit 17 of 16 (final capstone) · 2 weeks · ~250 min/week

Featured work: None external for the portfolio/exhibition strand. The "subject" of that strand is the student's OWN body of work from across the year (Dream Room, Contour Animal, Value Landscape, color still life, texture study, and so on). The new Careers in Art strand (see below) cites real, verified U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data — no artwork images involved.

Capstone deliverable / ladder rung: Curated Portfolio + Reflective Artist Statement + Virtual Exhibition — synthesis/reflection rung (no new artwork).

REVISION NOTE (this pass)

This is a revision of the 03_Development draft per the subject-matter reviewer's audit. One substantive addition was made: a new "Careers in Art" mini-lesson and Tier 1 research assignment. No other content in this unit was changed; the self-assessment-replaces-quiz structure, the VR "Hang Your Show" session, and the Capstone itself are untouched from the draft. Full detail on the addition follows below.

NEW: "Careers in Art" mini-lesson — what changed and why

What was added:

  • A new Part 4 · Look Ahead: Careers in Art section in lesson.html, placed after Part 3 (Watch It Work) and before the AI-awareness callout. It teaches students how to read a real career profile (typical education/skills, job outlook, work locations, typical pay), walks through one fully-worked example (Graphic Designer, sourced from the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, May 2024 data), shows an original CSS bar-chart comparison of median pay across five real careers, and lists four more real careers with direct links to their BLS profiles.
  • A new Week 1, Tier 1, completion-scored Canvas Assignment in canvas-items.md: "Careers in Art Research — Where the Toolkit Leads." Students pick 2–3 real art-related careers and build a comparison table (education/skills, job outlook, work locations, pay, cited source), using BLS OOH or O*NET OnLine. Two new vocabulary terms (Job Outlook, Median Wage) were added to the Vocabulary card grid, and the "What You'll Do Next" list was renumbered from 4 items to 5 to insert this assignment as item 2, ahead of the VR Session, Self-Assessment, and Capstone.

Placement decision and rationale:

Placed in Week 1, alongside the Portfolio Inventory, and before every Week 2 item, including the Capstone (per the assignment brief's requirement that it precede the portfolio capstone assignment). Three other placements were considered and rejected:

  • A standalone third week / extra sub-cycle — rejected. The course is built as a fixed 16 x 2-week cycle; adding a third week to the final unit alone would break the cycle length convention documented in build-conventions.md for no real pedagogical gain.
  • Folded into the Self-Assessment Checklist — rejected. That checklist is a quality-control pass against the capstone rubric; career research is a different kind of thinking (external, factual research vs. internal self-critique) and folding it in would muddy both.
  • After the Capstone, as a closing reflection — rejected. The assignment brief is explicit that this must sit BEFORE the capstone assignment, and pedagogically it works better before: students research real career data while they are already curating and evaluating their own body of work, so the "where does this lead" question lands while the "what did I actually build" question is fresh, rather than as a disconnected afterthought once the graded work is already submitted.

Landing it in Week 1 keeps the cycle's ONE-teacher-graded-assessment rule intact (it is Tier 1, completion-scored, like the Inventory, VR Session, and Self-Assessment) and keeps the total assignment count in Week 1 at two completion items, which mirrors the two-item Week 1 load already used in most other units of this course (sketch + VR, or similarly light pairs).

Standards gap this closes:

The reviewer's audit flagged a Florida/Texas standards gap: this course had no assignment addressing career awareness in art, despite both states' visual-arts standards explicitly naming it. This addition closes that gap:

  • Florida NGSSS: VA.912.H.3.1 — "Research and evaluate career opportunities in art and design fields." (Strand H, Historical & Global Connections — code verified against the working benchmark list in the optima-art skill's references/ngsss-68-912-benchmarks.md; description paraphrased, verify exact wording at cpalms.org before quoting in a formal alignment document.) VA.912.F.3.2 — "Investigate the role of artistic thinking and problem-solving in professional fields" — is a secondary match.
  • Texas TEKS (for cross-reference; this course is FL-primary): 19 TAC §117.302(c)(3)(D), Art I — "compare and contrast career and avocational opportunities in art," under the Historical and Cultural Relevance strand. Verified via the Texas Administrative Code (Chapter 117, Subchapter C, Fine Arts) as currently in force for Art, Level I.

Source verification (per copyright/fact-check policy):

All career and pay data is real, current, government-published data, verified this session via WebSearch against bls.gov before writing it into either file. No figure was estimated or invented.

  • Graphic Designers — median annual wage $61,300 (May 2024); middle 80% earn $37,600–$103,030; 2% projected growth 2024–2034; ~20,000 openings/year. bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/graphic-designers.htm
  • Art Directors — median annual wage $111,040 (May 2024); ~135,000 jobs in 2024; 4% projected growth 2024–2034; ~12,300 openings/year; typically bachelor's degree plus prior experience in another art/design occupation; fast-paced office environment. bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/art-directors.htm
  • Craft and Fine Artists — median annual wage $56,260 (May 2024); middle 80% earn $29,120–$133,220 (widest range of the five, reflecting heavy self-employment); little-or-no-change projected growth 2024–2034; ~4,400 openings/year; work in fine/commercial-art studios, home studios, or shared spaces. bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/craft-and-fine-artists.htm
  • Special Effects Artists and Animators (BLS's current title for the occupation formerly labeled "Multimedia Artists and Animators"; URL slug retains the old name) — median annual wage $99,800 (May 2024); middle 80% earn $57,220–$174,630; 2% projected growth 2024–2034; typically bachelor's degree in computer graphics, art, or related field. bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/multimedia-artists-and-animators.htm
  • Photographers — median annual wage $42,520 (derived from BLS's reported median hourly wage of $20.44, May 2024, on a full-time-equivalent basis); 2% projected growth 2024–2034; ~12,700 openings/year. bls.gov/ooh/media-and-communication/photographers.htm

The one BLS.gov link cited to students that could not be directly fetched for a live 200-check (bls.gov returns 403 to automated fetch tools; its content was confirmed instead through multiple independent WebSearch result snippets that quote the page directly and consistently) is the same set of five URLs above. All five are the standard, predictable BLS OOH URL pattern (bls.gov/ooh/arts-and-design/[occupation-slug].htm or bls.gov/ooh/media-and-communication/[occupation-slug].htm) and were confirmed as real, live search results returned directly by name, not guessed.

NGSSS benchmarks addressed (Q4 capstone set)

  • VA.912.C.3.3 — Use analytical and reflective skills to evaluate one's own artwork (the reflective artist statement, DAIJ turned inward).
  • VA.912.F.3.1 — Analyze and discuss how the body of work in a portfolio reflects the development of skills and ideas (curation across the year; portfolio as evidence of growth).
  • VA.912.O.1.4 — Select and analyze the use of structural elements of art and organizational principles across one's portfolio.
  • VA.912.S.3.5 — Organize, present, and reflect on a portfolio/exhibition of works as a culminating studio experience.
  • VA.912.H.3.1 (NEW this pass) — Research and evaluate career opportunities in art and design fields (the Careers in Art Research assignment).
  • VA.912.F.3.2 (NEW this pass, secondary) — Investigate the role of artistic thinking and problem-solving in professional fields.

This capstone deliberately revisits ALL seven Elements of Art and the Principles of Design rather than introducing new content in its portfolio/exhibition strand; it closes the standards arc opened in Unit 1. The new Careers in Art strand is the one piece of genuinely new content in this final unit, added specifically to close a standards gap the content quiz replacement had otherwise left unaddressed.

Pacing against the 250 min/week budget

Week 1 (Curate & Reflect ≈ 250–280 min): lesson page reading + Look Back visual (~45 min) · Portfolio Inventory worksheet, list + tag + select 6 to 8 (~60 min) · gather/re-photograph or re-export chosen pieces (~45 min) · Careers in Art Research: read Part 4 + look up 2–3 careers + build comparison table (~30 min, NEW) · begin drafting the reflective artist statement using the DAIJ-inward model (~90–100 min).

Week 2 (Build Exhibition & Finalize ≈ 250 min): VR "Hang Your Show" session, hang + docent tour (~50 min) · finalize and polish the artist statement (~60 min) · Self-Assessment Checklist quality pass + fixes (~40 min) · assemble and submit the capstone, confirm signatures and filenames (~100 min).

Note on the Week 1 overage: Adding Careers in Art Research pushes Week 1 roughly 30 minutes over the standard 250-minute target. This capstone unit already ran a heavier Week 1 than a typical cycle (drafting a full paragraph statement, per the original draft's own pacing note), so the addition is absorbed there rather than by cutting time from the Inventory or artist-statement drafting. If a teacher finds this consistently runs long, the "propose your own career" option in Part 1 of the assignment can be dropped (limit to the five menu careers only) to save a few minutes of the research step.

Self-assessment-replaces-quiz deviation (intentional, unchanged from the draft)

This is the ONLY unit in the course that does not include an 8-question auto-graded content quiz. A final-unit content quiz would assess no new material. In its place is a completion-scored Self-Assessment Checklist that mirrors the capstone rubric and serves as the student's last quality pass before submission. This is by design, not an omission. The tier load is now: Inventory (T1), Careers in Art Research (T1, NEW), VR (T1), Self-Assessment (T1) are completion-scored; the Capstone (T3) is the single teacher-graded item.

Teacher grading load

ONE teacher-graded pass this cycle: the Capstone (portfolio + reflective artist statement + exhibition evidence) on the 5-row, 20-pt capstone rubric. This is a richer submission than a normal unit, so budget ~8 to 10 min/student. Inventory, Careers in Art Research, VR, and Self-Assessment are completion-scored (a fast credit/no-credit or effort check, not a rubric pass). The capstone is the course's final grade; consider it the summative anchor for the year.

Copyright check (per OAO Copyright Policy 2026)

  • No third-party artwork appears in this unit. Every image in the portfolio and exhibition is the student's own work, created across the year. No museum images, no in-copyright artists, no PD embeds, no AI-generated images.
  • The only <img> on the lesson page is the Optima header owl logo (optima-assets). All other visuals on the page are original HTML/CSS/SVG built with the course design tokens (the "elements traveled" recap grid, and the new median-pay bar chart in Part 4).
  • The new Careers in Art section cites real U.S. government (BLS) data, which is public domain federal statistical data; no image or copyrighted material is embedded, only text and outbound links to bls.gov and onetonline.org.
  • AI-awareness callout is factual and unchanged: AI can format/lay out a portfolio but cannot reflect on growth or judge a strongest piece. No persuasive closer.
  • Reminder for teachers: students should only include their OWN work in the portfolio; if any student incorporated a master-copy study from earlier in the year, it should be labeled as a study after a named artist, consistent with the unit it came from.

Deployment notes

  • lesson.html → GitHub Pages, embed in Canvas via iframe (see canvas-interactive-widgets). Deploy-ready; no preview banner. Head/style/header/script copied verbatim from Unit-01 (byte-consistent brand shell); the new .career-menu, .career-row, and .paybar-* classes are additive, scoped only to Part 4, and do not touch any existing selector.
  • canvas-items.md → build each item Canvas-native. Inventory, Careers in Art Research, VR, and Self-Assessment as Canvas Assignments (or the Self-Assessment as a completion-marked survey); Capstone as a Canvas Assignment with file upload + text-entry and the 5-row rubric attached.
  • No content quiz to build this cycle (replaced by the Self-Assessment Checklist — see deviation note above).
  • Module intro/outro wrappers (Canvas-native quizzes) bracket the cycle per optima-canvas-assignments — built at module level, not in this unit folder. As the final module, the outro is a natural place for a course-closing reflection.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: One-Color Value Scale + Ball Plan
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Before you paint a ball in one color, you train your hand to stretch that color across its full range. Focus on effort and observation, not perfection. Do both parts on one sheet of paper (about 30 minutes total).

Part 1: One-Color Value Scale. Pick ONE color (any hue you like). Draw a row of 5 boxes, each about 1 inch wide. Box 1 is the lightest tint you can make (your color plus a lot of white). Box 5 is the darkest shade you can make (your color plus black). Make boxes 2, 3, and 4 even steps in between. Stay in the same hue the whole way. Label the row "Lightest tint" to "Darkest shade."

Part 2: Disco Ball Plan. Draw a quick thumbnail of a round disco ball, about palm-sized. Then:

  • Draw a small arrow showing where your light source is coming from (pick one direction and commit to it).
  • Lightly mark where the lightest tint will go (the side facing the light) and where the darkest shade will go (the side turned away).
  • Note your one chosen hue in writing.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U10_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, auto/completion-scored):

  • Both parts present on the sheet
  • Value scale shows 5 distinct steps in ONE hue
  • Ball plan shows a light-source arrow and marked light/dark areas
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Week 1 VR Session: Monochromatic Gallery Critique
assignments.html:
Before you enter: Have your vocabulary list and the four DAIJ steps (Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Judge) ready.

Choose your work. This week you pick the artwork yourself. Look up ONE of the real, verified monochromatic works below (or bring in a different single-hue work of your own choosing, teacher-approved), then pull an image of it into your VR space using your VR app's import or reference-image tool. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

  • James McNeill Whistler, Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1 ("Whistler's Mother"), 1871. Musee d'Orsay, Paris. Public domain.
  • James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket, about 1875. Detroit Institute of Arts. Public domain.
  • A single-hue work of your own choosing, teacher-approved.

Part 1: Look (about 10 min). Move close to your chosen work in VR. Using your VR drawing or note tool, place short notes beside it answering:

  1. Describe: What is shown, and what single hue is it built from?
  2. Analyze: Where is the lightest tint and the darkest shade? How does that value range build the form?
  3. Interpret: What mood does the one color create?
  4. Judge: Does the single-color choice work? Why?

Part 2: Experiment (about 10 min). Use your VR drawing or painting tool to pick ONE color, then make a row of marks running from that color made very light to that color made very dark. Try to keep the hue the same the whole way and only change how light or dark it is. This is the same tint-to-shade move you will paint this week.

Part 3: Respond (about 5 min). Answer aloud (record a short voice note) or in writing: "If you could use only one color for an entire painting, which hue would you choose, and what mood would it create?" If you are in a live session, share with a classmate and respond to one other answer.

Submit: Take a screenshot inside VR showing your chosen work, your notes, or your light-to-dark experiment, and upload it. (No screenshot tool? Write 2 to 3 sentences describing what you did.) Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading: Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Monochromatic Disco Ball + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have seen how Picasso built a whole figure and a whole mood from one color. Now do the same on a round object. Paint a disco ball using ONE hue only, stretched from its lightest tint to its darkest shade, so the ball reads as round and solid.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing or painting paper, and ONE color of paint with white and black to mix tints and shades (or one color of colored pencil or marker plus a white and a way to go darker). A digital painting app set to one hue with light/dark control is an equally accepted option.

The one rule: stay in a single hue. The only thing you may change is how light or dark that hue is.

Steps:

  1. Choose your one hue and your light-source direction. Commit to both before you start.
  2. Mix or set up your range: at least a light tint, the pure hue, and a dark shade. A middle value or two helps.
  3. Draw the circle, then build the value. Place the lightest tint where the light hits, the pure hue across the middle, and the darkest shade on the side turned away from the light.
  4. Add the disco-ball facets (small squares or diamonds) and shade each one to its place on the ball, lighter near the light, darker in the shadow. Keep the round overall form reading through the facets.
  5. Add a small cast shadow on the surface beneath, on the side away from the light, to ground the ball.
  6. Check your contrast: your lightest light and darkest dark should be clearly different so the ball does not go flat.
  7. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • Only ONE hue is used, varied by tint and shade
  • A clear, consistent light source
  • A full value range from light tint to dark shade
  • The ball reads as round and solid, not flat
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What hue did you choose, and where is your light source?
  • Name where you placed your lightest tint and your darkest shade.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished ball as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U10_MonoDiscoBall_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Mix Your Secondaries and Tertiaries
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Before you design a full wheel, you will prove to yourself how colors actually mix. Focus on careful mixing and clean labels, not on a polished picture (about 30 to 40 minutes).

Materials: any color media that mixes (paint, colored pencils, or markers) and the three primaries: red, yellow, blue.

Part 1: Make the secondaries. Mix and paint or color a swatch of each secondary color, then label it with the colors you combined:

  • red plus yellow,
  • yellow plus blue,
  • blue plus red.

Part 2: Make the tertiaries. Mix at least four tertiary colors by combining a primary with the secondary next to it. Swatch and label each one, for example "yellow plus orange equals yellow-orange."

Lay your swatches in a neat row or grid so the steps are easy to read.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U11_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, completion-scored):

  • Three secondary swatches are present and labeled with their two primaries
  • At least four tertiary swatches are present and labeled
  • Mixes are reasonably accurate (orange looks orange, green looks green)
  • Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Week 1 VR Session: Color and Pointillism Gallery Critique
assignments.html:
Before you enter: Have your color vocabulary and the four DAIJ steps (Describe, Analyze, Interpret, Judge) ready.

Choose your work. This week you pick the artwork yourself. Look up ONE of the real, verified color-relationship works below (or bring in a different work of your own choosing, teacher-approved), then pull an image of it into your VR space using your VR app's import or reference-image tool. You may choose any gallery Location you like.

  • Paul Signac, View of the Seine at Herblay, 1889. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Public domain. (A Pointillist harbor-and-river scene built from complementary color, orange against blue.)
  • Vincent van Gogh, Terrace of a Cafe at Night (Place du Forum), 1888. Kroller-Muller Museum, Netherlands. Public domain. (Warm yellows and oranges set against a deep blue night sky.)
  • A different color-rich work of your own choosing, teacher-approved.

Part 1: Look and critique (about 10 min). Move close to your chosen work, then step back. Using your VR drawing or note tool, place short notes beside it answering:

  1. Describe: What is literally shown?
  2. Analyze: Where do you see warm and cool colors? Can you find a complementary or analogous relationship the artist used?
  3. Interpret: What mood does the color create?
  4. Judge: Does the color choice work? Why?

Part 2: Look closer at Pointillism (about 6 min). If your chosen work (or another Pointillist work you find) is built from dots, move in until the dots separate, then back until your eye blends them. In a quick voice note or text note, explain in one or two sentences what optical color mixing is doing.

Part 3: Build a relationship (about 8 min). Use your VR drawing tool to place a small cluster of color that shows ONE relationship on purpose: either a complementary pair (two opposite colors set side by side) or an analogous group (three neighboring colors). Label which one you built.

Submit: Take a screenshot inside VR showing your chosen work, your notes, or your color cluster, and upload it. (No screenshot tool? Write 2 to 3 sentences describing what you did.) Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder.

Grading: Completion. Evidence of all three parts attempted.

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Color Wheel Design + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have studied how three primaries become twelve colors. Now design your own. Create an original, creative 12-color wheel that any artist could read, themed by something you care about.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper, pencil, and color media that mixes (paint, colored pencils, or markers). A digital drawing app is an equally accepted option as long as you mix or choose each hue yourself.

Your wheel must include:

  1. All 12 colors in correct order around the circle: 3 primaries, 3 secondaries, and 6 tertiaries.
  2. Accurate mixing. Each secondary and tertiary should clearly look like the mix it represents.
  3. At least one labeled color relationship. Mark one complementary pair (two opposite colors) OR one analogous group (three neighbors), and label which it is.
  4. A theme. This is what makes it yours. Your wheel can be made of leaves, planets, candies, sea creatures, buildings, anything, as long as the twelve colors stay correct and readable. Be creative with the shapes the colors live in.

Steps:

  1. Sketch your circle and divide it into 12 even sections.
  2. Place your three primaries first, evenly spaced. Mix and add the secondaries between them, then the tertiaries between those.
  3. Apply your theme to the shapes or imagery while keeping each color accurate and in order.
  4. Choose one relationship to highlight, then label it clearly.
  5. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • All 12 colors are present, correct, and in the right order
  • Secondary and tertiary colors are mixed accurately
  • One color relationship is shown and correctly labeled
  • The theme is creative and carried through with care
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What is the theme of your color wheel, and why did you choose it?
  • Which color relationship did you label, and where is it?
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished color wheel as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U11_ColorWheel_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Silhouette Thumbnails + Value Ground
assignments.html:
This sketch is your planning rung, not a finished artwork. The goal is to test ideas quickly before you commit to your final landscape. Focus on clear shapes and a clear focal point, not on polish. Do both parts on one sheet of paper (about 30 minutes total).

Part 1: Silhouette Thumbnails. Draw 2 to 3 small boxes, each about 3 inches wide. In each box, sketch a different silhouette scene that tells a tiny story (a city at dusk, a figure on a hill, sailboats, a forest). Fill your main shapes in solid so you can read them from the edge alone. Inside each box, mark with an arrow the one spot you want the eye to land first. That spot is your focal point.

Part 2: Value Ground. Below your thumbnails, draw one wide box and fill it with a value gradation: fade smoothly from your lightest pencil pressure on one side to your darkest on the other, with no hard line between. This is the kind of glowing ground Douglas placed behind his figures.

Label your focal point in each thumbnail and label the light and dark ends of your value ground.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U12_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, auto/completion-scored):

  • Both parts present on the sheet
  • At least 2 silhouette thumbnails with a marked focal point

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Storytelling Silhouette Landscape + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have read how Aaron Douglas told a whole story with flat dark shapes and a glowing light. Now build your own. Design and draw a silhouette landscape that tells a story: a scene made of flat silhouetted shapes, set on a value-gradient ground, with one clear focal point.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper, pencil and eraser, and a way to make solid dark shapes (black marker, ink, or heavy pencil). A value-gradient ground can be built with pencil, marker blending, or watercolor. A digital drawing app with layers is an equally accepted option.

What your scene must do:

  • Tell a story. Choose a moment a viewer can read: a journey, a homecoming, a city waking up, a person reaching a summit.
  • Use flat silhouette shapes. Fill your main objects solid, with little or no inside detail, so they read from the edge alone.
  • Build a value-gradient ground. Fade the background smoothly from light to dark so the light seems to glow behind your shapes.
  • Create one clear focal point (emphasis). Use contrast, such as the lightest area next to a dark silhouette, or shapes that point inward, so the eye lands first on the heart of your story.

Steps:

  1. Pick the strongest thumbnail from your Week 1 sketch, or plan a new scene.
  2. Lightly map where your value gradient will run and where your focal point will sit.
  3. Lay in the value-gradient ground first, light to dark, no hard line.
  4. Add your silhouette shapes on top, filled solid. Overlap them so the scene has layers.
  5. Sharpen the contrast around your focal point so the eye is pulled there.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The scene clearly tells a story
  • Shapes read as flat silhouettes from the edge alone
  • The ground shows a smooth value gradation
  • One focal point clearly wins the eye through contrast
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What story does your scene tell?
  • Where is your focal point, and what contrast did you use to build it?
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Symbolic Self-Portrait + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have seen how Kahlo turned a self-portrait into a map of who she was. Now make your own. Create a Symbolic Self-Portrait: a portrait of yourself that uses chosen symbols, color, and composition to express your identity. It does not need to be photo-realistic. It needs to be meaningful and built on purpose.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper, pencil and eraser, and your choice of color media (colored pencils, markers, or paint). A digital drawing app with layers is an equally accepted option. Any medium is allowed.

Requirements:

  • A recognizable self-portrait of you (any style, any medium).
  • At least three personal symbols placed around or within the portrait.
  • A clear focal point: your face should be where the eye lands first. Build it with size, contrast, or placement.
  • Color and motif unity: repeat a limited palette and at least one motif so the work reads as one design.
  • Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.
  • Optional enhancement: If possible, interview a family member or someone in your community about a symbol that represents them, and add that one symbol to your portrait alongside your own. This is not required. Your self-portrait fully meets the assignment without it.

Steps:

  1. Start from your sketch. Confirm your three or more symbols and what each one means.
  2. Lightly place your face first, large enough to be the focal point. Plan the symbols around it.
  3. Build emphasis on the face: make it the largest, brightest, or most central element, or aim other lines toward it.
  4. Choose a limited palette (about three to five colors) and repeat it across the work. Repeat one motif in at least two places to tie the work together.
  5. Develop your symbols so each is clear enough to read.
  6. Optional enhancement: Add an Interviewed Symbol. If you have access to a family member or someone in your community, interview them briefly: ask what one object, image, or symbol they feel represents them, and why. Add that single symbol into your self-portrait alongside your own, in a way that fits your composition and palette. This step is an addition to the project above, not a substitute for anything above it. If an interview is not possible for you right now, skip this step. Your self-portrait with your own three-or-more symbols, completed through Step 5, already fully meets this cycle's requirements.
  7. Sign your work and review it against the requirements before you submit.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The face reads as the clear focal point
  • At least three symbols are present and personally meaningful
  • A limited palette and a repeated motif give the work unity
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • Who are you in this portrait, and what mood or idea did you want?
  • Name at least two of your symbols and say what each one means.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?
  • If you completed the interview enhancement: name who you spoke with (a first name or a relation, such as "my grandmother" or "my neighbor") and the one symbol you chose to represent them.

Submit: Photograph or export your finished self-portrait as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U13_SymbolicSelfPortrait_LastName.

Note on the interview enhancement (Step 6): It is optional and does not change the total points possible (still 20). A student who completes only the required steps can still earn full marks in every row.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Grid Copy Warm-Up
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Artists train their eyes before their hands. The point is to learn to trust the grid, not to draw a perfect picture. Plan on about 30 minutes.

With a ruler and pencil, draw a light grid of equal squares directly over it, about 1 inch per square. Number the columns and letter the rows so you can find any cell quickly.

Part 2: Copy 2 to 3 cells exactly. On a separate sheet, draw an empty grid of the same number of squares, but make each square larger (for example, 2 inches). Pick 2 or 3 neighboring cells and copy ONLY what is inside each one: the light areas, dark areas, and edges. Do not look at the whole picture while you work. Match one box, then the next.

Beside your copied cells, write one sentence: "What was easier to copy when I only looked at one small square at a time?"

Submit: Photograph both sheets in good light (no shadow across the paper) and upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U14_Sketch_LastName.

  • At least 2 cells are copied onto a larger grid
  • The copied cells match the values and edges of the originals
  • The one-sentence reflection is present

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Grid Enlargement Drawing + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have seen how Chuck Close built a giant, unified portrait one square at a time. Now use the grid method yourself. Choose a reference image, grid it, and enlarge it accurately onto a larger grid, rendering the whole thing in value.

Materials (home-accessible): a reference image (a printed photo of an animal or a face works best), drawing paper at least twice the size of your reference, a ruler, pencils (a range of soft and hard pencils helps), and an eraser. A digital drawing app with layers and a grid overlay is an equally accepted option.

Steps:

  1. Choose and grid your reference. Pick a clear photo of an animal or a face. With a ruler, draw a light, even grid over it. Squares of about 1 inch work well. Label columns with numbers and rows with letters.
  2. Build the enlarged grid. On your large sheet, draw an empty grid with the same number of squares, but make each square larger (for example, double). Same number of cells, bigger cells. Keep the lines light.
  3. Copy cell by cell. Work one square at a time. Copy only the light areas, dark areas, and edges inside each cell. Do not draw "the whole face" or "the whole animal." Move box to box.
  4. Render in value. Shade each cell to match the reference, building a full light-to-dark range. Keep your values consistent from cell to cell so the squares fuse into one image.
  5. Let the grid disappear. Gently lift or erase the grid lines as you finish, or keep them very light, so the unified picture comes forward.
  6. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

Elements and principles focus: proportion (kept accurate by the grid), scale (your drawing is larger than the reference), line, shape, and value inside each cell, all building toward unity across the whole.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The enlarged image is accurate and in proportion to the reference
  • A full light-to-dark value range is built cell by cell
  • Values are consistent enough that the cells read as one unified whole
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible
  • The work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What did you choose to enlarge, and why?
  • Name one place where the grid kept your proportions accurate, and one cell that was hard to get right.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished drawing as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U14_GridEnlargement_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 1 Sketch: Horizon, Two Points, and Boxes
assignments.html:
This sketch is your practice rung, not a finished artwork. Perspective is a construction skill, and the only way to learn it is to build the bones first. Focus on clean, accurate lines, not on a pretty drawing (~30 minutes).

Work on one sheet of paper with a pencil and a ruler.

Step 1. Draw one straight horizontal line across the middle of your page. This is your horizon line.

Step 2. Mark one vanishing point near the left end of the line and one near the right end. Two points total.

Step 3. Draw a single vertical line somewhere between the two points. This is the front corner of your first box.

Step 4. From the top and bottom of that vertical, lightly draw a line to the left vanishing point and a line to the right vanishing point. Add two more verticals to close the box. You now have one box in two-point perspective.

Step 5. Repeat to draw 2 to 3 boxes in all, some above the horizon line and some below, so you can see how they tip differently depending on where they sit.

Keep all the true vertical edges perfectly upright, and send every other edge back to one of your two points.

Submit: Photograph your sheet in good light (no shadow across the paper). Upload as JPG or PNG. Save a copy to your OneDrive art portfolio folder: 2DArt_U15_Sketch_LastName.

Grading (completion + effort, auto/completion-scored):

  • ✓ A horizon line with two vanishing points is set
  • ✓ 2 to 3 boxes are constructed in two-point perspective
  • ✓ Verticals are upright and other edges run to the points
  • ✓ Genuine effort is visible

assignments.title: Week 2 Studio Project: Two-Point Perspective Cityscape + Artist Statement
assignments.html:
You have studied how Renaissance artists built deep, measured space, and you have practiced the bones in your sketch. Now build a place. Draw a cityscape or a castle scene in correct two-point perspective, viewed so that you are looking at a corner and the buildings recede toward two vanishing points.

Materials (home-accessible): drawing paper, a ruler, pencil and eraser, and your choice of finishing media (pen, colored pencils, markers, or paint). A digital drawing app with layers and a ruler tool is an equally accepted option.

Focus: space built through linear perspective, supported by line (your construction edges) and balance in the overall composition.

Steps:

  1. Draw your horizon line and place two vanishing points, one toward each side. Decide what your scene is: a city street, a town square seen from a corner, a castle and its walls.
  2. Draw the front vertical edge of your first and largest building. Run its top and bottom edges back to the two vanishing points. Close the building with more upright verticals.
  3. Add at least five structures in all (buildings, towers, walls, gateways). Keep every vertical upright and send every depth edge back to the correct vanishing point.
  4. Use the perspective to create depth: nearer structures are larger, farther ones shrink toward the horizon. Add windows and doors that also follow the vanishing points.
  5. Arrange your scene so the composition feels balanced. Decide whether you want calm symmetry or a more active, asymmetrical layout.
  6. Finish with your chosen media, then sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • A horizon line and two vanishing points clearly govern the scene
  • Verticals stay upright and orthogonals run consistently to the two points
  • The space reads as believable depth, with nearer things larger
  • The composition is balanced and complete
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible, and the work is signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What is your scene, and where did you place your horizon line and two vanishing points?
  • Name one place where keeping the perspective consistent was tricky, and how you solved it.
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

You have seen two ways an artist can make a page where words and picture work as one thing: building both together from scratch, and transforming an existing page. Now make your own, the second way. Create one finished illustrated blackout poetry page: keep a chosen set of words, black out the rest to form a short poem, and illustrate the page in mixed media so line, value, contrast, and unity all support the words.

Text requirement: read this first. You must build your page on ONE of these, and ONLY one:

  • a printed page from a public-domain source (a book, poem, or newspaper published before 1928, such as a page printed from Project Gutenberg or a public-domain newspaper archive), or
  • a page of text you wrote yourself.

Do NOT use a page from a copyrighted book, magazine, textbook, or website. Blacking out and illustrating a copyrighted page makes a derivative work you are not permitted to create or share. Public-domain and self-written text are the only allowed sources. Good places to find public-domain pages: Project Gutenberg (gutenberg.org), public-domain newspaper archives (such as the Library of Congress Chronicling America collection), or your own writing.

Materials (home-accessible): your chosen printed page, a dark marker, pen, or paint to black out text, and your choice of added media for illustrating (colored pencils, markers, ink, paint, or glued cut paper). A digital version built in a drawing app with layers, starting from a scan or typed page, is an equally accepted option.

Steps:

  1. Read your page and choose 4 to 8 words that, in reading order, make a short poem or phrase worth keeping.
  2. Lightly box your kept words so you do not cover them by accident.
  3. Black out the rest of the text. Let your covering have shape and rhythm; it does not have to be flat black.
  4. Illustrate the page in mixed media so the picture grows out of the poem's meaning. Use line to lead the eye between kept words.
  5. Build value and contrast so the kept words stay the easiest thing to find on the page.
  6. Build unity: repeat a color, shape, or kind of mark so the poem and the picture read as one page.
  7. Sign your work. Every finished artwork carries its artist's name.

What makes a strong artwork:

  • The kept words form a real short poem or phrase
  • Line, value, contrast, and unity are used on purpose
  • The illustration and the poem agree and read as one page
  • The source page is clearly public-domain or self-written
  • Care and craftsmanship are visible; the work is complete and signed

Artist Statement (type into the submission text box, 2 to 3 sentences):

  • What is your poem, and where did your page come from (public-domain source or your own writing)?
  • Name two elements or principles you used on purpose and where (for example, value contrast on the kept words, or a repeated color for unity).
  • What are you proud of, or what would you change?

Submit: Photograph or export your finished page as JPG or PNG, upload it, and type your Artist Statement in the text box. Save the file to your portfolio: 2DArt_U16_BlackoutPoetry_LastName.

assignments.title: Week 1 Portfolio Inventory: Gather and Tag Your Year

assignments.html:

assignments.title: Week 2 VR Session: Hang Your Show
assignments.html:
Your portfolio deserves a room. In this session you build a virtual exhibition of the works you chose on your inventory and walk it like a real gallery.

Before you enter: Have your 6 to 8 chosen pieces ready as image files (the photos or exports you saved this year). Have your inventory notes nearby. Open your VR space and choose any gallery Location you like.

Part 1: Hang the show (about 15 min). Bring your chosen images into your VR space and place them on the walls of your gallery. Curate the order on purpose:

  1. Put your strongest piece where a visitor's eye lands first.
  2. Arrange the rest so the show flows and the elements vary as someone walks through (do not cluster all your value pieces in one corner).
  3. Leave a little space between works so each one can breathe.

Part 2: Give the tour (about 10 min). Walk your hung show as if you were the docent. Record a short docent-style tour (voice or video) OR write a short walkthrough. As you pass each piece, say one sentence: what it is and which element it best shows. End at your strongest piece and say why it anchors the room. If you are in a live session, walk a classmate's gallery and leave one specific compliment.

Submit: Upload a screenshot of your hung exhibition, plus your short tour recording or written walkthrough. (No screenshot tool? Write 4 to 5 sentences describing your gallery, the order you hung it in, and why.) Save the screenshot to your portfolio folder; this is your "evidence of the virtual exhibition" for the capstone.

Grading: Completion. Evidence that the show was hung and toured.

assignments.title: Week 2 Self-Assessment Checklist: Is It Ready?
assignments.html:
You are about to submit the final work of the course. Before you do, score your own portfolio honestly against the same criteria your teacher will use. For each line, mark Yes, Almost, or Not yet, and fix anything that is not a Yes before you submit. There is no wrong answer here; this is your last quality pass.

Breadth: Elements and Principles

  • My 6 to 8 pieces, taken together, show a range of Elements (value, color, line, space, texture all appear somewhere).
  • At least a few Principles of Design (balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, unity) are visible across the set.

Craftsmanship growth

  • My set includes work that shows how my skill grew this year, not only my earliest pieces.
  • The images are clear, well-lit photos or clean exports, not blurry or cropped oddly.

Curation and cohesion

  • I chose for strength AND variety, not the same skill repeated.
  • I can say in one sentence why each piece earned its place.

Reflective artist statement

  • My statement names which elements and principles I handled best, with specific pieces.
  • My statement says which single piece is strongest and why.
  • My statement reflects honestly on how I grew, not just "I worked hard."

Completion and signatures

  • All chosen artworks are finished and signed.
  • I have evidence of my virtual exhibition (screenshot plus tour).
  • My files are named and saved to my portfolio folder.

assignments.title: Week 2 Capstone: Curated Portfolio + Reflective Artist Statement + Virtual Exhibition
assignments.html:
This is the final work of 2-D Studio Art. You will not make a new drawing. Instead you will present the year: choose your best, say honestly what it shows, and give it a room. Your submission has three parts.

Part A: The curated portfolio (your 6 to 8 works).

Upload clear photos or exports of the 6 to 8 pieces you selected on your inventory. Together they should show your strongest work AND a range of Elements and Principles. Every piece must be finished and signed.

Part B: The reflective artist statement (about one paragraph).

Type your statement into the submission text box. This is longer than the short statements you wrote during the year; aim for a full, honest paragraph (about 6 to 9 sentences). Run DAIJ on your own body of work:

  • Describe: what is in your portfolio (how many pieces, what kinds, what media).
  • Analyze: which Elements and Principles you handled best, naming specific pieces as evidence.
  • Interpret: how you grew this year as an artist, with at least one before-and-after comparison.
  • Judge: which single piece is your strongest, and exactly why it earns that spot.

Be specific. A reader should be able to look at your portfolio and find the evidence for every claim you make.

Part C: Evidence of your virtual exhibition.

Include the screenshot of your hung show plus your short docent tour (recording or written walkthrough) from the VR session.

What makes a strong capstone:

  • The portfolio shows breadth: a range of Elements and Principles, not one repeated skill.
  • The selection is curated, not random; the pieces hold together as a set.
  • The artist statement is specific, honest, and points to evidence in the work.
  • The exhibition is hung and presented with care.
  • Everything is complete, signed, and clearly presented.

Submit: Upload your 6 to 8 artwork files and your exhibition evidence, and type your artist statement in the text box. Save the full set to your OneDrive portfolio. Portfolio filename convention: 2DArt_U17_Portfolio_LastName.
